title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: equivocation on 'cause' — true/direct vs abusive/indirect; sun illuminates truly, its setting is only abusively cause of darkness
pass_a_gloss: Equivocation in this word cause has imposed upon our adversaries, or at least has supplied them occasion of imposing upon others. For in a twofold way something is wont to be called the cause of such an event or effect: Truly, directly, and properly, after the manner of that which influences unto producing the effect; Abusively, indirectly, improperly, after the manner of that which does not act unto prohibiting the effect: As the sun by its rising is truly and properly said to be the cause why the air is illuminated; by its setting it is improperly and abusively said to be the cause why it is darkened, only in this sense, because by its presence it would have put the darkness to flight.
pass_b_english: Equivocation on the word cause has trapped our adversaries — or at least given them occasion to trap others. Something is called cause of an event or effect in two ways: truly, directly, and properly, as what flows in to produce the effect; abusively, indirectly, improperly, as what does not act to block the effect. So the sun at rising is truly and properly called cause why the air is lit; at setting it is only improperly and abusively called cause why it darkens — merely because its presence would have put darkness to flight.
source_text: Aequivocatio in hoc vocabulo causae imposuit adversariis nostris, aut saltem suppeditavit illis occasionem imponendi aliis. Nam dupliciter aliquid dici solet causa talis eventus aut effectus: Vere, directe, et proprie, per modum influentis ad producendum effectum; Abusive, indirecte, improprie, per modum non agentis ad prohibendum effectum: Sicuti sol ortu suo vere et proprie causa dicitur cur aer illuminetur; occasu improprie et abusive causa dicitur cur obtenebretur, hoc sensu solummodo, quia sua praesentia tenebras fugasset.
